title: Zephyrine and the Recipe
premise: Ansel Okafor has spent four years at Maple Hollow High perfecting invisibility, counting the days until graduation frees him from a town of nine hundred people who either ignore him or whisper about him. When his history teacher pairs him with Zephyrine Vance—cheer captain, pastor's daughter, and the person who made freshman year unbearable—for a semester project on their town's founding, the two uncover a buried 1920s scandal: the town's revered founder stole the recipe (and the fortune) of a Black immigrant family, Ansel's own ancestors. As they dig deeper, Zephyrine must choose between her father's whitewashed legacy and the truth, while Ansel learns that staying invisible was a cage he built himself. The project ends with them presenting the real history at the Founder's Day centennial, costing Ansel his only friend and Zephyrine her family's standing—but earning them something rarer: justice, and each other, on the night of prom.
about_author: Quentin Amberdale is the pen name of a former small-town history teacher who spent a decade watching students discover that the past is never as tidy as the plaques claim. He writes YA contemporary fiction about outsiders who learn that truth-telling is a muscle, and lives in a restored farmhouse full of unreliable local archives.

chapters.title: The Counting Kid
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Opening on day 148 of his graduation countdown, we see Ansel's careful choreography of invisibility—lunch alone, routes mapped to avoid hall monitors and worse. His only friend, Dev, keeps him anchored. When Mr. Halloran announces semester partners for the local history project and reads 'Okafor and Vance,' the room goes quiet. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into panic.

chapters.title: Nemesis, Assigned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins. Zephyrine, reeling from her parents' separation and her father's demands for perfection, resents being paired with 'that kid who made everything weird in ninth grade'—a rumor she started and can't fully explain. Their first library session is armed truce. But Ansel's genuine knowledge of local archives surprises her. Emotional beat: reluctant curiosity breaking through hostility.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Wouldn't Say
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Digging through county records, Ansel finds a gap: his great-great-grandfather Ezekiel Okafor, a baker listed in the 1920 census, vanishes from every town document after 1923. Zephyrine's founder-ancestor, Cornelius Vance, opened his famous bakery that same year. Ansel shows her the dates; she flinches at the implication. Emotional beat: the first crack in the official story—and in their truce becoming alliance.

chapters.title: The Recipe Card
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Searching her grandmother's attic for centennial decorations, Zephyrine finds a recipe card in unfamiliar handwriting, annotated 'E.O.'—Ezekiel Okafor's signature sourdough, the recipe that made Vance's Bakery legendary. Her grandmother makes her swear to say nothing: 'Some histories are better left baked over.' Zephyrine hides the card but photographs it. Emotional beat: guilt and complicity taking root.

chapters.title: Detention and Confession
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Caught after hours in the historical society, Ansel and Zephyrine share detention, where she finally admits the freshman rumor was a lie she told to fit in. Ansel, stunned, admits he built his invisibility as armor. They agree: find the whole truth before the centennial. Dev warns Ansel he's setting himself up to be hurt again. Emotional beat: mutual vulnerability, fragile trust.

chapters.title: Fire and Ash, 1923
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The county archive yields a newspaper fragment: the Okafor family bakery burned in 1923, ruled accidental, family run out of town. Zephyrine's great-grandfather's diary hints Cornelius knew more. Meanwhile Pastor Vance announces his centennial sermon celebrating the 'Vance legacy,' pressuring Zephyrine to present the family's official history. Emotional beat: stakes rise from academic to personal; the past is a live wire.

chapters.title: The Sermon
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At Sunday service, Pastor Vance preaches on heritage and loyalty, staring directly at Zephyrine. Afterward she confronts him privately; he dismisses Ezekiel Okafor as 'a business dispute, long settled,' and forbids her to continue. She realizes he's known all along. She chooses the project—and Ansel—over obedience. Emotional beat: identity declared, family fracture begun.

chapters.title: Promises Before Prom
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel asks Dev to be his prom date, finally out loud, and Dev—terrified of his own visibility in a town this small—refuses and pulls away, their friendship cracking exactly as Ansel feared. Dev also threatens to expose the project as 'Ansel's grudge.' Zephyrine stands by Ansel publicly for the first time. Emotional beat: heartbreak and solidarity arriving together.

chapters.title: The Centennial
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the Founder's Day centennial, with the whole town assembled and Pastor Vance presiding, Ansel and Zephyrine present their project: the recipe card, the diary, the census gap, the fire. The crowd erupts; the mayor tries to cut the microphone; Zephyrine's grandmother, weeping, stands and confirms it. The town must reckon with its founding lie. Emotional beat: climax—truth spoken to power, cost and release at once.

chapters.title: What Rises
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, epilogue at prom. The fallout ripples: a historical commission, a formal apology to the Okafor family, Dev's halting apology and an uncertain but real step toward repair. Zephyrine finds Ansel in the gym, and they dance—not a romance sealed neatly, but a beginning. Ansel crosses out his countdown: he stopped counting. Emotional beat: resolution—identity claimed, justice imperfect but real, hope rising like dough.
